To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the aromatic residues of the fourth homology domain of voltage-gated Na channels contribute to local anesthetic inhibition through a cation-π interaction.
electrostatic interactions contribute significantly to local anesthetic binding at one site on voltage-gated sodium channel S6 segments.

the aromatic residues lining the pore of voltage-gated Na+ channels play an essential role in local anesthetic inhibition, and this role is facilitated by electrostatic interactions between the cationic drug and &pgr;-electrons on these residues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of voltage-dependent ion channels and their inhibition by local anesthetics.
understanding how local anesthetics work and how to improve their efficacy and safety.
understanding the molecular mechanism by which local anesthetics inhibit sodium channel function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

1) the aromatic rings of Phe1580 and Phe1579 are involved in the binding of local anesthetics to the sodium channels, and 2) the aromatic rings are involved in the electrostatic interaction of lidocaine with the sodium channels.
the electrostatic contribution of the aromatic residues in the local anesthetic receptor of voltage-gated Na+ channels is a cation-pi interaction.
the electrostatic contribution of Phe1578 and Phe1579 to local anesthetic binding is negligible, whereas Phe1579 plays an important role in the binding of lidocaine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that electrostatics are a major contributor to local anesthetic inhibition.
the aromatic residues in the local anesthetic receptor of voltage-gated Na+ channels are important in the mechanism of inhibition by local anesthetics.
aromatic residues in the S6 segment of domain 4 of voltage-gated Na channels contribute to the binding of local anesthetics by electrostatic interaction with the aromatic rings of the drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

electrostatic contributions to the inhibition of voltage-gate sodium channels by local anesthetics are highly site specific and depend critically on the local electrostatic properties of the aromatic residues that line the pore of the channel.
local anesthetics are not only interacting with the aromatic rings of the aromatic residues in the channel, but they are also interacting with the &pgr; electron clouds of these aromatic rings.

the electrostatic interaction of lidocaine with aromatic rings in the sodium channel is a major determinant of the potency of this drug and that this interaction is not shared with other drugs in the same class.
